title: 7. Listening Practice and Module Close
blocks: The full seven-level practice ladder — self-check, guided and independent drills, trap practice, and mixed Part 1 / Part 3 style mini-tests — plus the Module 1 wrap-up.

Everything in Module 1 has led here. Strategy that is only read is quickly forgotten; strategy that is practised becomes instinct. This file climbs the seven-level practice ladder, pulling together prediction, keywords, paraphrase, distractors, and every question type into one progressive workout.

A note on audio: a printed guide cannot play recordings, so most drills below give a short transcript to read at speaking pace, then answer. This trains the exact mental moves you need. For the top of the ladder, timed and full tests, apply this system to real audio. Keep your Error Log open the whole way through — every wrong answer gets a reason code.

items.prompt:
1. What single question do you ask of every gap before the audio?
2. Which three kinds of word are almost never paraphrased?
3. In the shape [decoy] + [signal] + [answer], where is the correct answer?
4. In multiple choice, what does hearing an option's words tell you?
5. When you miss an answer, what is the one thing you must not do?
items.answer: 1. “What kind of answer am I about to hear?” 2. Names, numbers, dates. 3. After the signal. 4. Almost nothing, until the speaker endorses it. 5. Chase it backwards while the audio moves on.

blocks.title: Drill 7.1: Prediction
blocks.instructions: For each gap, write the grammatical shape and information type.

items.prompt:
1. “The café seats about ____ people.”
2. “Bring a ____ in case it rains.”
3. “The session is led by Dr ____.”
4. “The castle dates from the ____ century.”
5. “Tickets are available from the ____ office.”
items.answer: 1. Number (a people count). 2. Noun, object (umbrella, coat). 3. Name (a surname). 4. An ordinal number (a century). 5. Noun, place/role before “office” (ticket, box, main).

blocks.title: Drill 7.2: Keyword anchors
blocks.instructions: Underline the single best keyword and label it (anchor, strong content, concept).

items.prompt:
1. “The library reopened in 2019 after refurbishment.”
2. “The main problem was a lack of parking.”
3. “Ask for Mrs Delgado at the desk.”
4. “The tour is popular with families.”
items.answer: 1. 2019, anchor. 2. parking, strong content (or “problem” as a concept warning of paraphrase). 3. Delgado, anchor (name). 4. popular, concept — expect a paraphrase like “families love it.”

blocks.title: Drill 7.3: Paraphrase
blocks.instructions: Try it first, then compare with the model answer.

items.prompt: Write one likely paraphrase for each: expensive, begin, difficult, close to.
items.answer: expensive: costly, pricey, dear. begin: start, get under way, kick off. difficult: hard, tricky, tough. close to: near, a short way from, within reach of.

blocks.title: Drill 7.4: Note completion
blocks.instructions: Try it first, then compare with the model answer.

items.prompt: Notes: Club name = ____ (1); Meets on = ____ (2); Cost per term = ____ (3); Bring your own = ____ (4). Transcript: “Welcome to the Riverside Photography Club. We meet every Thursday evening in the community hall. Membership is twenty-five pounds a term, which covers everything except that you'll need to bring your own camera, of course.” Write 1 to 4, obeying a two-word-and-or-a-number limit.
items.answer: 1. Riverside Photography (Club), trimmed to fit. 2. Thursday(s). 3. 25 pounds / twenty-five pounds. 4. (a) camera — “covers everything except” is the signpost that isolates what you must bring.

blocks.title: Drill 7.5: Multiple choice
blocks.instructions: Try it first, then compare with the model answer.

items.prompt: Q: “How did the speaker travel to the conference?” A) train B) car C) plane. Transcript: “I'd planned to fly, but the flights were so expensive that I ended up driving, which actually gave me a chance to see the countryside.”
items.answer: B, car. “Planned to fly” (plane) is the decoy; “but… I ended up driving” gives the answer. Choosing C because “fly” came first is the correction-trap error.

blocks.title: Drill 7.6: Name the trap
blocks.instructions: Every item here contains a distractor. Name the trap type (correction, two-number, rejected option, speaker attribution, negation) and give the answer.

items.prompt:
1. “The deposit's usually a hundred, but returning customers pay just seventy.”
2. “We'll meet at the library, actually the café is quieter, let's do that.”
3. “Which two are provided? Towels are, and a hairdryer, but soap you bring yourself.”
4. “Ravi thought the plan was risky; Mia disagreed, calling it perfectly safe.”
5. “The trip isn't cancelled, it's just been postponed to next week.”
items.answer:
1. Two-number trap. Answer: 70 (returning customers), decoy 100.
2. Correction trap. Answer: café, decoy library, signal “actually.”
3. Rejected-option trap. Answers: towels and a hairdryer; soap is denied.
4. Speaker-attribution trap. Ravi = risky, Mia = safe.
5. Negation trap. Answer: postponed to next week, not cancelled.

blocks: Level 5: Mixed practice (a Part 1 style mini-test)

blocks.title: Level 5 mini-test (Part 1 style)
blocks.instructions: Read once at natural speed: “Good morning, Greenfield Leisure Centre, how can I help? Hi, I'd like to book a badminton court. Can I take your name? It's Tomas Reinholt. That's R-E-I-N-H-O-L-T. And a contact number? It's 0-1-6-3-2, then 5-5-double-8-1-9. Which day would you like? Saturday, if possible. Morning. Saturday morning is fully booked, I'm afraid, but Sunday morning has space. Sunday's fine. Courts are nine pounds an hour, though before eleven it's a reduced rate of six pounds. We'll come at ten, so the cheaper one. And do we bring anything? Rackets can be hired for two pounds, but do bring your own indoor shoes, that's essential.”

items.prompt: Questions (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER): 1. Surname 2. Contact number 3. Day booked 4. Price per hour they will pay 5. Item they must bring
items.answer: 1. Reinholt (spelled out, get it exact). 2. 01632 55819 (note “double 8” is two eights). 3. Sunday — Saturday morning is “fully booked,” the decoy. 4. 6 pounds — nine pounds is the standard rate (decoy); “before eleven… six” plus “we'll come at ten” selects six. 5. (indoor) shoes — rackets “can be hired” (optional decoy); shoes are “essential.” If you missed the number, log it as SP or CL and slow down on digit strings; if you missed 3 or 4, log DS — both were two-option traps resolved by a later condition.

blocks: Level 6: Mixed question types (a Part 3 style mini-test)

blocks.title: Level 6 mini-test (Part 3 style)
blocks.instructions: Read once: “Tutor: So, your group project on renewable energy. Who's covering what? Nadia: I'll take solar power, it's what I know best. Kofi: I was going to do solar too, but since Nadia's on it, I'll cover wind. Leah: That leaves me with hydro, which is fine. Tutor: Have you decided on your main data source? Nadia: We looked at using a public survey, but the sample was tiny. Kofi: Right, so we're going with the government energy reports instead, they're much more reliable. Leah: Agreed, the reports it is.”

items.prompt: Matching: which topic does each student cover — 1. Nadia 2. Kofi 3. Leah? Multiple choice: 4. What data source did the group finally choose? A) a public survey B) government reports C) their own experiment.
items.answer: 1. Nadia = solar. 2. Kofi = wind (switched from solar because Nadia took it; the abandoned choice is the decoy). 3. Leah = hydro. 4. B, government reports — the public survey was considered but rejected (“the sample was tiny”); “going with the government energy reports instead” is the decision, confirmed by “the reports it is.”

blocks: Level 7: Full test (applying the system to real audio)

A printed guide cannot give you a full listening test with sound, and a “transcript-only” full test is not the real thing, because reading removes the pressure the test is built on. For Level 7, use real audio at real speed, played once, and apply the Module 1 system exactly:
In every pre-audio pause, predict the shape of each gap and set your keyword anchors.
Play the audio once only. Never pause or replay during a timed run.
Capture answers immediately, obey word limits, and trust the completion answers as exact words.
Treat every “but, actually, sorry, instead” as a distractor alarm.
If you miss one, reset cleanly and move on.
Afterwards, mark it, then fill your Error Log with a reason code for every mistake.

Do your full tests at the same time of day as your real exam, in one sitting, with no pausing. Your brain needs to rehearse not just the questions but the stamina. Students who only ever practise one section at a time are often shocked by how tired they are by Part 4 on test day.
Module 1 wrap-up: the Listening mindset, in one breath

Before each part, predict every gap and set your anchors. During the audio, listen for meaning, ride the signposts, and wait for the verdict before you commit. Treat every “but, actually, sorry, instead” as an alarm. Capture answers instantly and obey the word limit. When you miss one, reset and move on without a backward glance. Afterwards, log every mistake by reason, and drill the reason that dominates.

That is the whole module. Not “listen carefully,” but a precise sequence of decisions you can now run on demand. When you can do this without thinking, you are no longer hoping to catch answers — you are waiting for them, exactly where you knew they would be.
